notes.meaning: God explains that the people of Judah are completely fixed on their idolatry. Just as words carved with a diamond-tipped iron chisel into hard rock cannot be wiped away, their love for false gods is carved deep inside their thoughts and displayed on the corners of their pagan altars. Their sin is no small slip; it has stained both their inner desires and their public worship.

The parents in Judah have practiced idol worship for so long that their children grow up knowing all about it. Whenever they see a leafy green tree or a high hill, they think of the wooden poles set up for the Canaanite goddess Asherah and the altars built to Baal. The bad example of the older generation has passed down deep into the next generation.

God addresses Jerusalem and the temple hill as His mountain in the open country. Because the people filled the land with pagan hilltop shrines, the Lord will allow invading armies to carry off the city's treasures and wealth as stolen goods. The very places they used for worshiping idols will bring about their ruin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the Hebrew phrasing here is difficult and may have suffered damage in copying, closely matching the warning in Jeremiah 15:13.

notes.meaning: The people will lose the Promised Land that God gave to their ancestors as a precious inheritance. Because of their continuous rebellion, they will be dragged away to serve foreign masters in a distant, unfamiliar country. Their actions have lit the fire of God's holy anger, which will burn against them like an unquenchable flame.

The Lord declares a warning against relying on mere human strength rather than on Him. When Judah looked to military treaties with countries like Egypt instead of trusting God, they were leaning on fragile human flesh. Walking away from the living God to depend on people always brings spiritual ruin.

differ.view: This verse shows the danger of relying on human free will and our own moral efforts for salvation rather than depending wholly on God's grace in Christ.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early teachers like Augustine used this verse to argue against Pelagius, teaching that human nature is too frail to achieve righteousness without the inner help of divine grace.

notes.meaning: Anyone who trusts only in human strength is compared to a stunted, lonely bush in the dry wilderness. Because it has no fresh water, it shrivels in the barren salt plains and cannot enjoy the good rain when it arrives. In the same way, a person who shuts God out ends up spiritually dry, lonely, and empty.

In contrast to the dry shrub, the person who trusts fully in the Lord receives rich blessings. Such a believer is like a healthy tree planted beside a flowing river, sending its roots deep into the moist soil. Even when scorching heat and dry seasons arrive, its leaves stay green, and it never stops bearing good fruit because God supplies all its strength.

The human heart is naturally crooked and full of tricks, leading people to fool even themselves about their true motives. It suffers from a deep spiritual sickness that no human effort can fix. Because our own desires can easily lead us astray, no person can fully understand how fallen their own heart really is.

differ.view: This verse teaches total depravity, meaning sin has corrupted every part of human nature so thoroughly that no one can turn to God without His sovereign work.
While this describes the fallen human heart apart from grace, believers in the new covenant receive a new heart and the Holy Spirit, even though a struggle with indwelling sin remains.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars suggest this verse belongs directly with verse 14 as Jeremiah's personal lament about his own inner weakness, which God answers in verse 10.

notes.meaning: Even though people cannot fully know their own hearts, the Lord sees into every hidden corner of the mind and conscience. He tests our secret motives the way a metalworker tests silver. Because He knows the truth about everyone, He will reward or judge each person fairly according to their real deeds.

Jeremiah uses an old country saying about a partridge sitting on eggs it never laid. When the chicks hatch, they quickly run off to their real mother, leaving the bird empty-handed. In the same way, someone who gets rich through cheating and dishonesty will lose those riches halfway through life and end up looking like a fool.

The prophet turns his eyes to the Lord, describing His heavenly presence and temple as a magnificent royal throne. Long before human kingdoms existed, God reigned in supreme glory. Finding security in His sanctuary is far better than trusting in money, idols, or human power.

The Lord is the true hope of Israel, but those who abandon Him will face shame and disappointment. People who turn away from God will have their names written in loose dust, blown away and forgotten by the wind. They have foolishly walked away from the Lord, who is the only spring of fresh, life-giving water.

Jeremiah cries out to God to cure his sorrow and rescue him from his enemies. He knows that if the Lord heals and saves him, he will be truly and completely safe. God alone deserves all his praise because only divine power can bring full relief.

The people mock Jeremiah because the disasters he predicted have not happened yet. They taunt him by asking where God's threats are and daring the Lord to bring them right away. Because God was being patient and giving them time to turn back, the scoffers assumed the warnings were false.

Jeremiah defends himself before God, stating that he never ran away from his job as a shepherd and prophet to his people. Even though he had to announce terrible judgment, he never wished for the day of disaster to arrive. God knows that every word Jeremiah spoke came directly from the Lord and not from personal hatred.

The prophet pleads with God not to let His presence become another source of terror to him. With hostility coming from all sides, Jeremiah desperately needs the Lord to be his safe shelter when trouble strikes. Having God on his side is the only thing that keeps him from being overwhelmed.

Jeremiah asks God to bring shame and defeat upon the people trying to harm him, while keeping him safe from disgrace. He calls for the promised day of judgment to break the power of his stubborn persecutors with complete destruction. This prayer is an appeal for God's justice to vindicate His faithful word against those who mock it.

The Lord tells Jeremiah to go and preach at the city gates of Jerusalem, including the gate used regularly by the kings. These gates were busy public places where crowds gathered and daily business was done. Jeremiah was to call out to the rulers, citizens, and travelers alike, demanding that they listen to God's message.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historical-critical scholars argued that the Sabbath sermon in verses 19–27 was inserted by a later editor to support the Sabbath reforms found in Ezra and Nehemiah.

notes.meaning: God commands the people to take care and stop carrying heavy loads through the city gates or out of their homes on the Sabbath day. The fourth commandment required Israel to treat the seventh day as holy by resting from normal weekly labor and business trade. Turning God's special day of rest into an ordinary market day showed deep disrespect for His covenant.

differ.view: These verses show that God requires a strict, full day of rest from worldly labor and business, a moral duty that continues for Christians on the Lord's Day.
The Sabbath rules here were part of Israel's old covenant ceremonial law, serving as an obedience test for Judah rather than a binding rule for New Testament church worship.

notes.meaning: The Lord reminds them that their ancestors refused to listen to this command in past generations. Instead of accepting God's correction, they became stubborn and stiffened their necks in rebellion. The current generation was simply repeating the bad habits of their parents.

God offers Judah a fresh start if they will genuinely turn back to Him and honor the Sabbath by stopping their business traffic. If they obey, the Davidic monarchy will continue in strength, and their kings will ride in royal chariots through the city gates. Jerusalem will remain secure, peaceful, and lived in forever.

If the nation honors God, worshippers will stream into Jerusalem from all across the kingdom, including the hill country, the plains, and the southern Negev desert. They will arrive at the temple bringing animal sacrifices, grain offerings, incense, and thank offerings. Obedience would bring back joyful, full worship throughout the entire land.

The chapter closes with a serious warning: if the people refuse to keep the Sabbath holy and keep hauling goods through the gates, God will ignite an unquenchable fire in those very entrances. That fire will burn down the palaces and fortresses of Jerusalem. This warning came true decades later when Babylonian soldiers broke in and burned the entire city.

differ.view: Presbyterian and Puritan traditions have preached these verses as an enduring principle, teaching that societies and churches flourish or decline depending on whether they treat the Lord's Day as a holy Sabbath set apart from worldly trade and labour.
Other evangelicals treat this strict Sabbath command as a specific covenant test meant only for Old Testament Israel, which does not bind the Christian church under the new covenant.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars suggest this passage about the Sabbath was not part of Jeremiah's original ministry, but was added later by editors after the exile to encourage the Sabbath reforms described in Ezra and Nehemiah.
